title: Count Almost Equal Pairs II
statement:
Two positive integers are *almost equal* when they can be made equal with at most two operations in total (both on the same number, or one on each). One operation picks one of the two numbers and exchanges two of its digits. After an operation a number keeps all of its digit positions even if it now starts with `0`; leading zeros do not change its value, so `0213` equals `213`.

Given an array `nums` of positive integers, return how many index pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` have `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` almost equal.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying swaps on both numbers of every pair is too slow. Two facts help. First, every swap can be moved onto the longer number: line the numbers up with leading zeros on the shorter one; if swapping two positions of `y` makes it equal to `x`, then swapping the same two positions of `x` makes it equal to `y`. Second, a number has few variants: with at most 7 digits there are 21 single swaps, so at most 21 + 21² results of two swaps. So sort `nums`; every earlier number is then no longer than the current one, and only the current number's variants need looking up among them.

## Approach

1. Sort `nums` in increasing order.
2. For each `num`, split it into `digits` and compute `place`, the power of ten of each position.
3. Swapping positions `i` and `j` changes the value by `gain(i, j)`, so one swap gives `once = num + gain(i, j)`.
4. Apply that swap to `digits`, add `once + gain(p, q)` for every second swap `(p, q)`, then undo the first swap.
5. Add the `count` of each value in the set `variants` to `pairs`, then record `num` in `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted, `nums = [213, 1023, 2130, 2310]`.

- `213`: nothing earlier; `count` now holds `213`.
- `1023`: swapping its first two digits gives `0123`, then swapping the `1` and `2` gives `0213 = 213`, so `pairs = 1`.
- `2130`: neither `213` nor `1023` is a variant (each needs three swaps).
- `2310`: one swap reaches `2130`; two swaps reach `1023` and `0213`. `pairs = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n + n·d⁴), where d ≤ 7 is the digit count: each number tries about (d²/2)² pairs of swaps.
- Space: O(n + d⁴) for `count` and one number's `variants`.

## Pitfalls

- Swapping only inside the shorter number misses pairs: `1` cannot change, but `100` can become `001`.
- Different swap sequences often give the same value; collect them in a set first so each earlier number counts once.
- Undo the first swap before trying the next one, or later variants start from the wrong digits.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | how many times each earlier number appeared |
| `pairs` | almost-equal pairs found so far |
| `num`, `digits`, `len` | the current number, its digits and their count |
| `place` | the power of ten of each digit position |
| `gain` | how much the value changes when digits `i` and `j` swap |
| `variants` | values `num` reaches with at most two swaps |
| `once` | the value after the first swap |
